              I.   INTRODUCTION

         Staff’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief provides no basis to disapprove, rewrite, or narrow the

ten-party Comprehensive Stipulation. The record establishes that the Stipulation resulted from

serious bargaining among capable and knowledgeable parties representing diverse interests;

benefits customers and the public interest; violates no important regulatory principle or practice;

and produces fair, just, and reasonable rates. The Commission should approve the Stipulation in

its entirety and without modification. 1

         Although Staff acknowledges the Commission must evaluate the Stipulation as an

“integrated package,” 2 its brief does the opposite. Staff isolates disputed provisions, compares each

provision to Staff’s litigation position, and asks the Commission to substitute Staff’s preferred

terms in place of the negotiated bargain. Staff’s approach ignores the integrated bargain that

balances give and take on the revenue requirement, allocation, rate design, customer protections,

cost recovery, and implementation terms. Staff may have struck a different bargain but has not

shown that the bargain the Signatories reached is unfair, unreasonable, or contrary to the public

interest.

         Staff’s objections fall into three principal groups. First, Staff challenges the support for the

stipulated $90 million increase and argues that developments during the case make SPS’s Future

Test Year unreliable. Second, Staff asks the Commission to substitute its own $47.7 million

revenue-deficiency calculation, which uses historical data to allocate shared system costs while



         1

ignores that NMDOJ is a Signatory, and that New Mexico law directs the Attorney General to “represent residential
and small business consumers in matters before the public regulation commission as the attorney general deems
appropriate.” NMSA 1978, § 8-5-17(A); SPS Ex. 49 (Rebuttal Testimony of Alexander G. Trowbridge in Support of
Comprehensive Stipulation (“Trowbridge Stip. Reb.”) at 27–28. Staff also ignores that all of the customers and
customer groups involved in this proceeding support the Stipulation.
         2
           Staff Initial Br. at 5.

                                                            1
 retaining Future Test Year revenues and billing determinants. Third, Staff attacks individual

negotiated terms concerning Cunningham BESS, class allocation, PTCs, and several accounting

and cost-recovery issues. None of Staff’s arguments justifies rejecting or rewriting the Stipulation.

       Staff’s attack on the stipulated $90 million increase rests on two mistaken premises. Staff

calls the stipulated result a “black box” because Staff mistakenly calculated $35.9 million in

allegedly unexplained reductions. But Staff’s calculation omitted several key adjustments,

including the removal of BESS LTPPA capacity costs and Southwest Power Pool deficiency

payments, revised depreciation expense, and zero cash working capital. If Staff had accounted for

those adjustments, only $1.963 million separates the identified cost-of-service result from the

negotiated $90 million increase as Exhibit A to Staff’s brief now reflects. The record thus shows

where the identified adjustments end and the final negotiated compromise begins. Accordingly,

Staff’s “black box” characterization is belied by Staff’s own revised calculation.

       Staff also treats corrections and updates involving discrete Future Test Year components as

proof that SPS’s entire Future Test Year filing cannot be trusted. That reasoning turns the Future

Test Year Rule on its head. The Rule expressly permits forecasts and provides a process for

correcting them as information develops. SPS followed that process. Staff identifies no error in

SPS’s financial load forecast and offers no alternative forecast. Instead, Staff conflates changes in

depreciation expense and resource adequacy with a change in forecasted customer load.

Authorized corrections to one part of a Future Test Year case do not discredit forecasts that Staff

has not shown to be wrong. The Commission should reject Staff’s effort to treat the Rule’s

established update process as a reason to distrust SPS’s Future Test Year filing.

       Although Staff attempts to rely on the Commission’s Final Order in Case No. 25-00066-

UT, that decision does not support Staff’s Future Test Year theory. That proceeding addressed the



                                                 2
 future allocation of specific generation, storage, and transmission projects. The Commission

directed SPS not to rely on projected or speculative load growth “alone” when allocating those

projects; it did not impose a historical-data requirement on SPS’s systemwide financial load

forecast or displace the Commission’s Future Test Year Rule. Staff therefore cannot transform a

project-specific instruction into a general rule against the use of supported forecasts in this rate

case.

        Staff’s alternative $47.7 million revenue-deficiency calculation is internally inconsistent

and should be rejected. As Section III explains, Staff would replace SPS’s Future Test Year

allocation data with historical data while retaining Future Test Year revenues and billing

determinants. In other words, Staff assumes forecasted New Mexico growth will occur when

calculating SPS’s revenues, but assumes that same growth will not occur when allocating costs to

New Mexico. When SPS applies historical data consistently to both sides of the calculation, the

resulting revenue deficiency is approximately $173.1 million, not $47.7 million. That mismatch

undermines Staff’s proposed $47.7 million result and provides no basis to replace the negotiated

$90 million increase.

        Staff’s objections to individual Stipulation terms are equally unpersuasive. On the

Cunningham BESS, Staff agrees that New Mexico customers should receive all associated benefits

if they bear the directly assigned costs; the dispute is over how to measure those benefits. Staff

mistakes the planning reserve margin (“PRM”) adjustment for a second reduction to

Cunningham’s capacity value. Accredited capacity (“ACAP”) reflects the amount of Cunningham

capacity that Southwest Power Pool counts for resource-adequacy purposes, while the PRM

adjustment determines how much peak load that capacity can support while maintaining the

required reserve. Cunningham’s energy-arbitrage and ancillary-service benefits separately flow to



                                                 3
 New Mexico customers through Southwest Power Pool market settlements and the FPPCAC. The

Stipulation therefore gives New Mexico the full Cunningham benefit without overstating the

amount of shared system capacity that Cunningham replaces.

        Staff’s class-allocation objection has narrowed even further. Staff now acknowledges that

“the true point of disagreement” is the overall revenue requirement, not the Stipulation’s banding

methodology. At the stipulated $90 million increase, Dr. Blank testified that he had “no problem

with the banding.” Staff’s lower bill impacts thus reflect its lower overall revenue deficiency, not

a materially different class-allocation method. Staff’s disagreement with the overall revenue

requirement provides no basis to modify the negotiated class allocation.

        Staff’s PTC objections fail for similar reasons. Its proposed ten-year limit on PTC carrying

charges confuses the period during which a facility may generate new credits with the period an

individual credit may remain unused and accrue carrying charges. Staff’s allocation argument rests

on a different flawed premise. AED-4CP allocates fixed production costs based in part on peak

demand, while PTCs are earned from qualifying kilowatt-hours of electricity. Energy-at-Source

therefore ties the benefit to the energy production that creates the credits and adjusts for line losses.

Staff’s PTC objections do not justify modifying the negotiated treatment.

        Staff’s remaining accounting and cost-recovery objections likewise reflect preferences for

different amounts or recovery periods, not grounds for modifying the Stipulation. Section 1.5

authorizes no present recovery of short-term capacity costs or Southwest Power Pool deficiency

payments; it caps any New Mexico deferral at $10 million annually and leaves prudence and

recoverability for later review on an actual record. The stipulated ELI treatment uses the updated

$26.2 million balance – not the approximately $28 million balance Staff attacks – and a three-year

amortization that falls between SPS’s proposed two years and Staff’s four. Staff’s rate-case-



                                                   4
 expense reduction relies heavily on the outcomes of only two prior cases rather than the demands

of this proceeding. Finally, the stipulated legacy-meter and Community Solar treatments already

extend SPS’s proposed recovery periods from two to four years, materially reducing annual rate

impacts. These disputes do not show that the negotiated terms are unreasonable.

       In sum, Staff asks the Commission to reconstruct a ten-party settlement around the

litigation positions of the one party that opposes it. Staff has identified terms it would have

preferred but has not shown that the integrated bargain before the Commission is unlawful,

unreasonable, or contrary to the public interest. The Commission should approve the Stipulation

in its entirety and without modification.

           II.   THE RECORD ANSWERS THE QUESTIONS RAISED AT HEARING

       A. “Fair, Just, and Reasonable” States a Unitary, End-Result Standard.

       As SPS explained in its Initial Brief, “fair, just, and reasonable” establishes a single,

flexible ratemaking standard. A just and reasonable rate balances customer and investor interests

and falls within the “zone of reasonableness” between utility confiscation and ratepayer extortion. 3

The Commission evaluates the rate order’s total effect; “[t]he result reached, not the method

employed,” controls. 4 “Fair” does not impose a separate ratemaking test—the term’s ordinary

meaning substantially overlaps with “just.” 5

       Staff’s brief acknowledges this basic principle, 6 but then proceeds provision by provision,

asking whether Staff would have chosen a different amount, amortization period, allocation




       3
         N.M. Att’y Gen. v. N.M. Pub. Regul. Comm’n, 2011-NMSC-034, ¶¶ 13, 16–17.
       4

 method, or recovery mechanism for individual terms. 7 Staff’s approach ignores the governing

standard. The question is not whether every provision independently reflects Staff’s preferred

result, but whether the negotiated package, taken as a whole, produces fair, just, and reasonable

rates. For the reasons set forth below, it does.

        B. Different New Mexico and Texas Retail Rates Do Not Make New Mexico Rates
           Unfair or Unreasonable.

        New Mexico and Texas may reasonably set different retail rates for customers served by

SPS’s integrated system. Each state regulates retail service under its own laws and ratemaking

framework. New Mexico permits use of a Future Test Year, while Texas relies on historical data in

base-rate cases and relies on separate riders to recover certain costs between rate cases. The states

may also approve different depreciation rates, returns, capital structures, allocation methods, and

rate designs. Those differences affect when and how customers pay SPS’s costs. As Mr.

Trowbridge explained, comparing the two states is “not entirely simple.” Customers may share an

electric system without paying identical retail rates. 8

        Staff now agrees with this basic conclusion. It expressly states that its recommendation

does not “require Texas and New Mexico customers to pay identical rates.” 9 Staff instead argues

that the Commission should use historical data to allocate certain shared system costs to New

Mexico. That separate argument is addressed in Section III, infra. The question Chair O’Connell

raised is whether different rates, standing alone, make New Mexico rates unfair. They do not. The

a stipulation resolves disputed issues is reasonable. It does not say that each provision must be severed from the
negotiated bargain and independently reproduce Staff’s litigated result.

        The Hearing Examiners also raised two narrower questions concerning PTC treatment.

They asked how long SPS should earn carrying charges on unused, transfer-eligible PTCs, and

whether Energy-at-Source fairly allocates PTC benefits among customer classes. For the reasons

set forth in Section IV.C, infra, the Commission should adopt SPS’s two-year limit on PTC

carrying charges and approve the stipulated Energy-at-Source allocation.

        III.     THE $90 MILLION STIPULATED INCREASE IS SUPPORTED, AND
                 STAFF’S FUTURE-TEST-YEAR OBJECTIONS DO NOT UNDERMINE IT

        A. The $90 Million Stipulated Increase Is Supported and Transparent.

        As SPS explained in its Initial Brief, the Commission ultimately judges rates by looking at

their total effect. Ratemaking requires “pragmatic adjustments,” and “the result reached, not the

method employed,” controls whether rates are fair, just, and reasonable. 10 The question, then, is

whether the stipulated rates fall within the zone of reasonableness and fairly balance customer and

investor interests. 11

        They do. The Stipulation does more than reduce SPS’s requested base-rate increase by

$85.4 million. It also supports the $90 million result and shows how the parties got there. Before

the parties reached the Stipulation, SPS had already updated its filed revenue deficiency under

17.1.3.19(C) NMAC, reducing it by approximately $3.05 million and providing supporting

workpapers and an updated, fully functional cost-of-service model. 12 The Stipulation then set the

agreed $90 million increase, identified the specified cost-of-service terms underlying the

        Staff nevertheless continues to characterize the stipulated amount as a “black box” and “not

        B. The Future Test Year Rule Expressly Permits Forecasts and Corrections.

       The Future Test Year Rule is expressly forward-looking. It allows a utility to establish the

Future Test Year revenue requirement through “adjustments, forecasts, budgets or other reasonable

methods.” 20 It also requires linkage data demonstrating a “verifiable link” between historical base-

period data and future-test-year data. 21 The Rule anticipates that forecasted inputs may change.

Section 17.1.3.19 establishes procedures for revisions arising from errors, changes in law, or

changed circumstances; requires a utility to present nonmaterial revisions in a comprehensive list

so the adjustments remain verifiable; and permits additional corrections through rebuttal

testimony. 22 SPS followed that process here. Its March 20 Comprehensive List identified

corrections, new information, and changed circumstances and quantified their effect. 23

       Staff nevertheless argues that linkage data “must be actual provable number[s]” because

“[t]he only way a utility can verify or validate” a Future Test Year is to provide actual numbers. 24

Staff’s reading conflicts with the Rule’s text. The Rule requires a verifiable link between historical

data and the forecast; it does not require the forecast itself to become historical data. Indeed,

requiring “actual numbers” would largely write “forecasts” and “budgets” out of the Future Test

Year Rule and render the Rule meaningless.

       Nor do SPS’s post-filing corrections show that the original Future Test Year revenue

requirement “did not reliably represent” expected conditions or justify broader skepticism toward

every unrevised input. 25 Section 17.1.3.19 anticipates that new information and changed

circumstances may require corrections during a forward-looking case. SPS used the prescribed

the Rule’s correction mechanism worked as intended.

       C. Staff Identifies No Error in SPS’s Financial Load Forecast.

       Staff identifies no error in SPS’s financial load forecast. Instead, it points to corrections or

updates involving depreciation expense and resource adequacy and treats those changes as grounds

to discredit the entire Future Test Year filing. 26 But depreciation, the financial load forecast, and

resource adequacy involve distinct inputs and measure different things. Depreciation determines

an accounting expense. The financial load forecast projects the sales, energy, and demand SPS

expects during the Future Test Year. Resource adequacy measures the capacity SPS expects to

have available to meet system requirements. A change in one does not establish an error in another.

Staff identifies no error in SPS’s financial load forecast and offers no alternative forecast.

       Staff’s changing capacity-deficiency figures illustrate the flaw in its reasoning. A capacity

deficiency is a resource-adequacy result, not a load forecast. Forecasted load affects that result,

but so do capacity purchases, outages, resource availability, and resource accreditation. 27 Thus, the

fact that SPS’s projected capacity deficiency changed from the figure used when it prepared the

case does not establish that forecasted load changed or identify any error in the financial load

forecast. Mr. Gable’s testimony that he did not know whether SPS had updated the financial

forecast does not supply that missing proof. Staff presented no contrary evidence and declined to

cross-examine Dr. John Goodenough, SPS’s forecasting witness.

       Besides conflating three separate forecasts, Staff’s reasoning also conflicts with the Future

Test Year Rule’s plain language. Section 17.1.3.19 expressly allows SPS to correct or update its

filing as information develops. It defines revisions that change the originally filed jurisdictional


       26
            Staff Initial Br. at 13–17.
       27
            Staff Initial Br. at 14–16.

                                                 10
 revenue deficiency or surplus by less than 5% as immaterial and permits SPS to present them

through a comprehensive list rather than a modified application. 28 SPS’s March 20 revisions

reduced its originally filed deficiency by only 1.74%, and Staff identifies no violation of the Rule’s

revision procedures. 29 Staff cannot turn SPS’s use of the Rule’s prescribed correction process into

evidence that an otherwise unchallenged forecast is unreliable. That reasoning would make the

correction mechanism self-defeating: every authorized correction made to improve the Future Test

Year would instead become a reason to distrust the forecasts that remain unchanged.

        Nor does Case No. 25-00066-UT support Staff’s theory. That proceeding concerned CCNs

for approximately $9.38 billion of new generation, storage, and transmission projects and related

project-specific ratemaking principles. The Commission approved the resources but deferred

general jurisdictional allocation of six Self-Build Projects until a later base-rate case, when it could

evaluate actual system usage and project benefits on a full record. 30 The Commission did not apply

the Future Test Year Rule to SPS’s systemwide financial load forecast or prescribe historical data

as the required measurement period in a Future Test Year rate case. And paragraph 105 says only

that SPS may not rely on projected or speculative load growth “alone” to support jurisdictional

allocation of those projects. 31 It does not transform a project-specific directive into a rule requiring

historical data whenever a forecast changes.

        Staff’s reliance on the changing revenue deficiency estimate has another flaw: the estimate

changed, in part, because the Stipulation removed the projected Southwest Power Pool deficiency

payment from the stipulated revenue requirement. Section 1.5 withdraws immediate FPPCAC

recovery and permits only the deferral of actual short-term capacity costs or deficiency payments

        Accordingly, Staff offers no evidence that SPS’s financial load forecast is wrong. It relies

forecast unreliable. That argument conflicts with the Future Test Year Rule and should be rejected.

        D. Staff’s Alternative Revenue-Requirement Analysis Is Internally Inconsistent.

        Staff’s argument is that the jurisdictional allocators set forth in the Comprehensive

Stipulation present a mismatch with those used by Texas and are thus not supported or result in

rates that are not fair, just, and reasonable. 33 Staff’s contention is wrong. The fact that jurisdictions

may differ in their approach to regulatory ratemaking does not establish that different rates between

those jurisdictions are unfair or unreasonable. 34 Despite the differences that may arise in timing

and how customers in different jurisdictions pay shared system costs, SPS filed an FTY, consistent

with the PUA, the FTY Rule, and Commission precedent, designed to establish rates that will

reflect the costs SPS expects to incur, the loads it expects to serve, and the system conditions

expected during the period when new rates will be in effect. 35 Staff’s approach simply does not

establish rates that reflect these conditions.

        Staff recognizes that different proposed jurisdictional allocators are the reason for the

significant difference between the revenue deficiency proposed by Staff and the revenue deficiency

         IV.     STAFF’S OBJECTIONS TO INDIVIDUAL STIPULATION TERMS DO
                 NOT JUSTIFY MODIFYING THE INTEGRATED AGREEMENT.

        A. The Cunningham BESS Treatment Reasonably Directly Aligns Assigned Costs
           with Corresponding Project Benefits.

        Staff agrees with the basic premise of the stipulated Cunningham BESS treatment: if New

Mexico customers pay Cunningham’s directly assigned costs, they should receive 100% of the

resource’s benefits. 44 The Stipulation does exactly that. It credits Cunningham’s capacity value

through an adjustment to New Mexico’s 12-CP allocator, while Cunningham’s actual energy-

arbitrage, market, and ancillary-service benefits flow to New Mexico customers through the

FPPCAC. 45 Staff challenges that treatment on both procedural and substantive grounds. Neither

has merit.

        Staff first argues that the PRM adjustment was not adequately vetted because it first

appeared in the Stipulation and Staff did not have an opportunity to conduct discovery on it. 46 But

Staff identifies no discovery request it served after the Stipulation was filed, no request for an

expedited response, and no request for additional time that was denied. Moreover, Staff was invited

to the settlement meetings, most of which it did not attend, and, after the Stipulation was filed,

submitted detailed opposition testimony on the PRM adjustment. Staff had a meaningful

opportunity to test the provision or propound discovery on it. That Staff failed to do so provides

no basis to reject Section 1.3.

        Staff’s substantive objections likewise do not undermine the stipulated treatment. Staff

contends that because the formula adjusts Cunningham’s accredited capacity (“ACAP”) to account

twelve monthly system peaks, so the Stipulation applies the appropriate seasonal ACAP and PRM

values to each monthly peak. 51 Nor is SPS performing a separate resource-adequacy analysis for

Cunningham. It is measuring the effect of a directly assigned resource on New Mexico’s

responsibility for shared production capacity. Staff’s observation that SPS manages resource

adequacy for its portfolio as a whole does not answer that allocation question.

         V.       CONCLUSION

       For the reasons set forth above and in SPS’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief, the Stipulation

satisfies the Commission’s criteria for approval. It resulted from serious bargaining among capable,

knowledgeable parties; benefits customers and the public interest when viewed as a whole; violates

no important regulatory principle or practice; and produces fair, just, and reasonable rates. Staff’s

Brief shows that Staff would have preferred a different result, but it does not show that the

integrated agreement the Signatories reached is unreasonable. The Commission should therefore

approve the Stipulation in its entirety and without modification.
